patterns.name: app-shell
patterns.intent: Assemble a full authenticated app screen by dropping the primary nav, optional secondary menu, global search, and page content into the App Shell's slots.
patterns.description: The sanctioned way to build a top-level screen: an `AppShell` whose sidebar slot holds `SidebarPrimary` (and, when a section has sub-navigation, `SidebarSecondary` beside it), whose header slot holds `SearchGlobal` plus account/actions, and whose main slot holds the routed page content. App Shell is a slot-based layout — it owns only the structure (full-height row, sticky header, independently scrolling main); the rich behavior comes from the components placed in the slots.
when_to_use: The root frame of an authenticated application screen.
Screens that need persistent primary nav + a global header across routes.
when_not_to_use: Marketing or auth screens — use the (future) Auth Layout.
A region within a page — use Section / Stack / Grid.
anti_patterns: Hand-rolling a fixed sidebar/header with raw divs instead of the AppShell slots (loses the landmark semantics and sticky/scroll behavior).
Putting page content in AppShellHeader, or more than one AppShellMain (breaks the single `main` landmark).
Styling the scaffold with custom colors instead of letting SidebarPrimary / SearchGlobal own their tokens.

patterns.name: auth-screen
patterns.intent: A centered authentication screen (sign-in / sign-up / reset) built on AuthLayout with a card-framed form and a footer link.
patterns.description: The sanctioned way to build an authentication screen: `AuthLayout` centers the page and holds an `AuthLayoutCard` framing a short form of `InputText` fields and a full-width primary `Button`, with a `Link` (forgot-password / switch to sign-up) in the `AuthLayoutFooter`. One recipe covers sign-in, sign-up, and reset — only the fields, the submit label, and the footer link change. Composes existing components rather than a bespoke login screen.
when_to_use: Any unauthenticated entry screen — sign-in, sign-up, password reset, MFA challenge.
A short, focused form the user completes before entering the app.
Keeping the branding + form centered and consistent across all auth variants.
when_not_to_use: A settings or profile form inside the authenticated app — use a page layout, not `AuthLayout`.
A multi-step onboarding flow — use `wizard-dialog` or a routed sequence.
A modal credential prompt over existing content — use a `Dialog`.
anti_patterns: Hand-centering a card with ad-hoc flexbox instead of composing `AuthLayout` (loses the shared logo/footer slots and responsive framing).
Putting more than the essential fields in the card — auth screens stay short; defer everything else to inside the app.
Using a raw `<a>` for the footer link instead of `Link`, breaking focus-ring and color tokens.
Making the submit button anything but full-width primary — the single obvious action is the point.
patterns.example:
function SignInScreen({ onSubmit }) { return ( Sign in
Forgot password? ); }

patterns.name: card-grid
patterns.intent: A responsive grid of uniform cards (catalog / gallery / overview tiles) under a page header.
patterns.description: The sanctioned layout for a set of peer items shown as tiles: a `PageHeader` over a responsive `Grid` of uniform `Card`s. `Grid`'s `cols` variant handles the responsive column counts, so every tile aligns and reflows consistently without ad-hoc CSS grid. Use it for catalogs, galleries, product/plan pickers, and overview tiles — anywhere the items are homogeneous cards rather than tabular rows.
when_to_use: A collection of peer items best shown as uniform cards (catalog, gallery, plan picker).
Content that should reflow responsively from one column to several.
An overview page where each tile links into a detail view.
when_not_to_use: Tabular records with columns to sort/filter/paginate — use `table-view`.
A widget dashboard of heterogeneous, differently-sized panels — use the `dashboard` pattern (including its container-query grid inside the AppShell main region).
A single prominent item — a lone `Card` needs no grid.
anti_patterns: Rolling a bespoke CSS grid instead of composing `Grid` (loses the kit's responsive column tiers and gap tokens).
Mixing wildly different card heights/contents so the grid reads as a broken table — keep tiles uniform.
Cramming dashboard widgets into a uniform card grid — heterogeneous panels belong in `dashboard`.
Omitting the `PageHeader`, leaving the grid without a title or context.
patterns.example:
function CatalogGrid({ items }) { return (
Integrations Connect the tools your team already uses. {items.map((item) => ( {item.name} {item.summary} ))}
); }

patterns.name: confirm-dialog
patterns.intent: A modal confirmation for a discrete, often destructive action — AlertDialog with a title, description, and cancel / confirm actions.
patterns.description: The sanctioned way to make a user confirm a single, consequential action: an `AlertDialog` with a `AlertDialogTitle`, a short `AlertDialogDescription` stating the consequence, and exactly two footer actions — an `AlertDialogCancel` and an `AlertDialogAction` (styled `destructive` when the action is irreversible). `AlertDialog` is deliberately more insistent than a plain `Dialog`: it traps focus, defaults focus to the safe choice, and cannot be dismissed by clicking outside — the point of a confirmation. Composes the primitive rather than a bespoke confirm modal.
when_to_use: Confirming a destructive or irreversible action (delete, revoke, disconnect).
A yes/no decision with a clear consequence and no data to enter.
Interrupting a risky flow so the user must acknowledge before proceeding.
when_not_to_use: A non-destructive inline toggle or setting — apply it directly, don't gate it behind a dialog.
Anything that collects input (even one field) — use `form-dialog`.
A routine, reversible action — a `toast` with undo is friendlier than a modal.
anti_patterns: Using a dismissible `Dialog` (click-outside closes) for a destructive confirm — reach for `AlertDialog`, which won't dismiss accidentally.
More than two actions in the footer — a confirmation is binary; extra choices belong elsewhere.
Focusing the destructive action by default — default focus stays on Cancel.
A vague description ("Are you sure?") that hides the consequence instead of naming it.
patterns.example:
function DeleteConfirm({ open, onOpenChange, onConfirm, name }) {
  return (
    <AlertDialog open={open} onOpenChange={onOpenChange}>
      <AlertDialogContent>
        <AlertDialogHeader>
          <AlertDialogTitle>Delete {name}?</AlertDialogTitle>
          <AlertDialogDescription>
            This permanently removes {name} and its data. This action cannot be undone.
          </AlertDialogDescription>
        </AlertDialogHeader>
        <AlertDialogFooter>
          <AlertDialogCancel render={<Button variant="ghost">Cancel</Button>} />
          <AlertDialogAction render={<Button variant="destructive">Delete</Button>} onClick={onConfirm} />
        </AlertDialogFooter>
      </AlertDialogContent>
    </AlertDialog>
  );
}

patterns.name: dashboard
patterns.intent: Build a dashboard screen by laying widgets into a container-query Grid inside the App Shell's main content.
patterns.description: The sanctioned way to build a dashboard: an `AppShell` (primary nav + header) whose main holds a `PageHeader` and a `Grid` of widgets. The Grid uses `container` so the widget columns respond to the main content's width — which shrinks as the sidebar expands — rather than the viewport. There is no dedicated "DashboardLayout" component: a dashboard is App Shell + a container Grid of widgets (e.g. WidgetPlaceholder / Card), which is this composition.
when_to_use: Overview / dashboard screens made of a grid of widget cards.
when_not_to_use: A general two-dimensional layout outside a variable-width area — a plain `Grid` (viewport breakpoints) is enough.
Non-grid page content — use `Section` / `Stack`.
anti_patterns: Reaching for a bespoke "dashboard layout" component — it's just App Shell + a container Grid (this pattern).
Using a viewport-breakpoint Grid inside App Shell main — the columns won't account for the sidebar width; use `<Grid container>`.

patterns.name: data-table-bulk-actions
patterns.intent: Select rows in a data table and act on the selection via a contextual bulk-action bar.
patterns.description: The sanctioned way to offer row selection with bulk actions (delete, export, …): a checkbox selection column drives a contextual bar that replaces the toolbar while rows are selected, showing the count and the available actions. Because the bulk bar and the row checkboxes must read the SAME selection state, this composes the Table primitives + DataTablePagination over a single `useReactTable` instance — not the self-contained `DataTable` (which owns its own internal state and can't share selection with external chrome).
when_to_use: A table where users pick several rows and apply one action to all of them.
Destructive or batch operations (delete, export, assign) on multiple rows.
when_not_to_use: A read-only or single-select table — use `DataTable` directly.
One action per row — put a row action (menu / button) in a cell instead.
anti_patterns: Using the self-contained `DataTable` and a separate `useReactTable` for the bar — their selection states diverge.
Leaving the bulk bar always visible — show it only while rows are selected.
Hiding the selection count — always show "N selected" so the scope is clear.
patterns.example:
const table = useReactTable({ data, columns, // includes a checkbox 'select' column getCoreRowModel: getCoreRowModel(), getPaginationRowModel: getPaginationRowModel(), enableRowSelection: true, onRowSelectionChange: setRowSelection, state: { rowSelection }, }); const selected = table.getSelectedRowModel().rows; {selected.length > 0 ? (
{selected.length} selected
) : ( )} {/* render table.getHeaderGroups() / getRowModel() */}

patterns.name: detail-drawer
patterns.intent: Show details of a selected item in an edge-anchored Drawer — header, key/value properties, content states, and footer actions.
patterns.description: The sanctioned way to present "details of the selected thing" in a non-blocking, edge-anchored `Drawer`: a header (title + close), a body that renders either a `DescriptionList` of key/value properties or a content state (loading → `Spinner`, empty/error → `Empty`), and a footer of `Button` actions, with a `Separator` framing the footer. This is the `Drawer`-based sibling of `sheet-detail-panel`: reach for **detail-drawer** when the panel is a lightweight, dismissible surface anchored to a screen edge (built on the `Drawer` primitive); reach for **sheet-detail-panel** when you want the modal, dialog-based `Sheet` (focus-trapped, backdrop, scroll-locked). Same content recipe, different overlay primitive.
when_to_use: Inspecting a selected row/entity in a panel that slides in from a screen edge.
A detail view that must load, can be empty, and offers a few actions.
A non-blocking inspector the user can leave open while scanning the list.
when_not_to_use: A modal, focus-trapped detail panel with a backdrop — use `sheet-detail-panel` (the `Sheet` variant).
A centered confirmation or short form — use `confirm-dialog` or `form-dialog`.
Persistent page chrome that never dismisses — use `SidebarSecondary`, not a Drawer.
anti_patterns: Hand-rolling a fixed edge panel instead of composing `Drawer` (loses the swipe/dismiss, animations, and ARIA wiring).
Rendering a spinner/empty state inline in the body INSTEAD of switching the whole body by a content state — mixed states confuse.
Putting more than ~2–3 primary actions in the footer; overflow belongs in a menu.
Omitting `DrawerTitle`, leaving the panel with no accessible name.
patterns.example:
function DetailDrawer({ open, onOpenChange, contentState, item }) { return ( {item?.name ?? 'Details'} {contentState === 'loading' ? (
) : contentState === 'empty' ? ( Nothing to show This item has no details yet. ) : ( {item.properties.map((p) => ( {p.label} {p.value} ))} )} Close} /> ); }

patterns.name: empty-screen
patterns.intent: Show a full-screen zero state inside the App Shell when a page has no content yet.
patterns.description: The sanctioned full-screen empty state: an `AppShell` (primary nav + header) whose main centers an `Empty` (icon + title + description + optional action). Use it for first-run / no-data screens so the chrome stays consistent while the content area communicates the empty state. The sidebar configuration (expanded / collapsed / with a secondary nav) is independent — see the App Shell stories.
when_to_use: A page that has no data yet (first run, filtered-to-nothing, not-set-up).
when_not_to_use: An empty region inside an otherwise full page — use `Empty` on its own.
A loading state — use a `Spinner` / `Skeleton` in place of the content.
anti_patterns: Replacing the whole shell with a bare centered message (loses the nav/header chrome and the user's place in the app).
Using `Empty` without centering it in the main area — it should sit in the optical center of the content region.

patterns.name: field-group
patterns.intent: A set of related choice controls under one legend — a CheckboxGroup, a RadioGroup, or a run of Switches.
patterns.description: The sanctioned way to present a group of related controls as one labelled unit. A `FieldSet` wraps the group and a `FieldLegend` names it (the group's accessible name); inside sits exactly one kind of control set: a `CheckboxGroup` of `Checkbox`es for multi-select, a `RadioGroup` of `Radio`s for single-select, or a stack of `Switch`es for independent toggles. The group is the validation unit — one `FieldError` under the set covers "pick at least one". Use horizontal/responsive `Field` orientation for label-left settings rows.
when_to_use: Several checkboxes/radios that answer one question ("Which channels?", "Plan?").
A block of on/off settings that belong together.
You want one legend + one error for the whole group, not per control.
when_not_to_use: A single standalone checkbox or switch — use a plain `Field` + `Checkbox`/`Switch`.
More than ~7 options, or options needing search — use `Select`/`Combobox`.
Mutually exclusive options where one must always be set — a `RadioGroup` with a default, not checkboxes.
anti_patterns: A group of checkboxes with no `FieldSet`/`FieldLegend`, so screen readers hear orphaned controls.
Mixing checkboxes and radios in one group, or using checkboxes for mutually-exclusive choices.
Putting the error on each control instead of once under the set.
Reaching for `FieldError` under a `FieldSet` — it needs a `Field.Root` ancestor; surface the group message directly (or wrap the group in a `Field`).
Hand-managing an array of booleans instead of letting `CheckboxGroup` own the `string[]` value.

patterns.name: filter-popover
patterns.intent: A trigger button that opens a popover containing filter fields with Apply / Reset actions.
patterns.description: The sanctioned way to offer multi-criteria filtering of a list or table without leaving the page: a Button opens a Popover holding a small form of select fields, with a primary Apply and a ghost Reset in a right-aligned footer. Composes existing components — no bespoke widget. Supersedes the legacy `el-multi-search`.
when_to_use: Filtering a table or list by a few discrete criteria (status, region, type).
Keeping filter controls tucked away until the user wants them.
when_not_to_use: A single always-visible filter — render the field inline instead of a popover.
Free-text search — use a search field (InputSearch / SearchGlobal), not selects.
A blocking, full-screen task — use a Dialog.
anti_patterns: Building a one-off dropdown panel by hand instead of composing Popover.
Putting destructive or navigation actions in the footer (only Apply / Reset).
Auto-applying on every change AND showing an Apply button — pick one model.

patterns.name: form-dialog
patterns.intent: A short create/edit form inside a modal Dialog, with a titled header and a cancel / submit footer.
patterns.description: The sanctioned way to capture a short create/edit form without leaving the page: a `Dialog` whose body holds a `Form` of `Field` + `InputText` controls, a header naming the task, and a footer with a ghost cancel and a primary submit. `Form` owns validation and error wiring; each `Field` binds a control to its label and error slot. Keep it to a handful of fields — the modal is for a quick, focused entry, not a whole page of inputs.
when_to_use: Creating or editing a small record (a few fields) without a full-page route.
A focused entry task the user should finish or cancel before continuing.
Reusing one form for both create and edit by seeding default values.
when_not_to_use: More than a single step — use `wizard-dialog`.
A whole page of fields or complex layout — use a dedicated route, not a dialog.
A yes/no or destructive confirmation with no input — use `confirm-dialog`.
anti_patterns: Wiring validation and error messages by hand instead of using `Form` + `Field`.
Submitting on backdrop click or losing entered data when the dialog closes — confirm or preserve the draft.
Overfilling the modal so it scrolls endlessly — if it needs that many fields, it's a page.
Omitting `DialogTitle`, leaving the dialog without an accessible name.
patterns.example:
function CreateProjectDialog({ open, onOpenChange, onSubmit }) {
  return (
    <Dialog open={open} onOpenChange={onOpenChange}>
      <DialogContent>
        <DialogHeader>
          <DialogTitle>New project</DialogTitle>
          <DialogCloseButton />
        </DialogHeader>
        <Form onFormSubmit={onSubmit}>
          <DialogBody className="flex flex-col gap-4">
            <Field name="name">
              <FieldLabel>Name</FieldLabel>
              <FieldControl render={<InputText placeholder="Acme migration" required />} />
              <FieldError />
            </Field>
            <Field name="key">
              <FieldLabel>Key</FieldLabel>
              <FieldControl render={<InputText placeholder="ACME" />} />
              <FieldDescription>A short identifier used in URLs.</FieldDescription>
            </Field>
          </DialogBody>
          <DialogFooter>
            <DialogClose render={<Button variant="ghost">Cancel</Button>} />
            <Button type="submit">Create</Button>
          </DialogFooter>
        </Form>
      </DialogContent>
    </Dialog>
  );
}

patterns.name: form-layout
patterns.intent: A full-page vertical form — a Form of labelled Fields grouped into titled sections, with a submit action.
patterns.description: The sanctioned skeleton for a page-level form: a single `Form` owning a stack of `Field`s, each pairing a `FieldLabel`, a control (`InputText`, `InputTextArea`, `Select`, …), an optional `FieldDescription`, and a `FieldError` slot. Related fields are grouped under a `FieldSet` + `FieldLegend`. `Form` collects values by each Field's `name` and validates on submit; a primary `Button type="submit"` (optionally a ghost cancel) closes the form. Fields stack vertically at a consistent gap — this is the base every other form pattern (`form-two-column`, `form-validation`, `field-group`) specializes.
when_to_use: A create/edit form that owns a whole page or a dedicated route.
More fields than fit comfortably in a `form-dialog`.
You want label↔control↔description↔error wiring handled for you (no manual `htmlFor`/`aria-*`).
when_not_to_use: A handful of fields in a modal — use `form-dialog`.
A multi-step flow — use `wizard-dialog`.
A dense side-by-side layout is required from the start — start from `form-two-column`.
anti_patterns: Hand-wiring `htmlFor`/`id`/`aria-describedby` instead of letting `Field` associate the parts.
Placing a bare `<input>` next to a floating `<label>` outside a `Field`.
Grouping unrelated fields under one `FieldSet`, or omitting `FieldLegend` so the group has no accessible name.
Inconsistent gaps between fields — let `Form`'s stack own the rhythm.
patterns.example:
function ProfileForm({ onSubmit }) { return (
Profile Full name } /> Bio } /> Shown on your public profile.
); }

patterns.name: form-two-column
patterns.intent: A responsive multi-column form — Fields laid out in a grid that collapses to one column on narrow viewports.
patterns.description: A longer form (profile, settings, billing) laid out as a responsive grid of `Field`s: two columns when there's room, one column when space is tight, so no field is ever cramped. Built on `form-layout` — same `Form` + `Field` validation wiring — but the paired fields sit in a `Grid` (use `container` so the columns respond to the form's own width, not the viewport). Full-width fields (a textarea, a wide `Autocomplete`) and the submit row live in the `Form`'s own column, outside the grid, so they naturally span the full width.
when_to_use: A form long enough that a single column would scroll excessively.
Naturally paired fields (first/last name, city/postcode) that read well side by side.
Settings/profile pages on wide layouts that must still work on mobile.
when_not_to_use: Short forms (≤4 fields) — a single column (`form-layout`) is calmer.
Inside a narrow dialog or drawer — keep one column.
Fields with long labels/help text that would misalign across columns.
anti_patterns: A fixed multi-column grid that doesn't collapse, forcing horizontal scroll on mobile.
Splitting a single logical field (label + control) across two columns.
Forcing a full-width field (textarea, wide picker) into a single column — keep it outside the grid.
Different row heights making the two columns drift out of alignment.
patterns.example:
function AccountForm({ onSubmit }) { return (
First name } /> Last name } /> Notes } />
); }

patterns.name: form-validation
patterns.intent: Inline field validation with accessible error messages — native Form/Field validity or a schema resolver.
patterns.description: How the kit surfaces validation. Each `Field` wires its control to a `FieldError` slot; an invalid field flips `data-[invalid]` and shows the message in the danger color, associated via `aria-describedby`. Two sanctioned approaches share the same markup: (1) **native** — let Base UI `Form` + `Field` run HTML constraint validation (`required`, `type="email"`, `pattern`) plus a per-field `validate` on submit/blur, choosing which message to show with `FieldError match`; (2) **schema** — drive `Field`'s `invalid` from a `react-hook-form` + `zod` `Controller` and render `fieldState.error.message`. Optionally reflect a derived score (e.g. password strength) with a `Meter`.
when_to_use: Any form where input must be checked before submit.
You need accessible, per-field error messages tied to the control.
Cross-field rules (password confirmation) — reach for the schema approach.
when_not_to_use: A field with no failure mode (freeform notes) — don't invent validation.
Server-only validation with no client rules — still use `Form`'s `errors` to surface them, but skip client `validate`.
anti_patterns: Showing a red border with no message, or a message not linked to the control.
Validating aggressively on every keystroke before the user has finished (prefer `onBlur`/`onSubmit`).
Rolling a bespoke error `<div>` instead of `FieldError`, losing the `aria-describedby` wiring.
Blocking submit silently — always move focus/scroll to the first invalid field.
patterns.example:
function SignUpForm({ onSubmit }) {
  return (
    <Form onFormSubmit={onSubmit} className="max-w-sm">
      <Field name="email">
        <FieldLabel>Email</FieldLabel>
        <FieldControl render={<InputText type="email" required placeholder="you@example.com" />} />
        <FieldError match="valueMissing">Email is required.</FieldError>
        <FieldError match="typeMismatch">Enter a valid email address.</FieldError>
      </Field>
      <Field
        name="password"
        validate={(value) =>
          String(value).length < 8 ? 'Use at least 8 characters.' : null
        }
      >
        <FieldLabel>Password</FieldLabel>
        <FieldControl render={<InputText type="password" required />} />
        <FieldError />
      </Field>
      <Button type="submit">Create account</Button>
    </Form>
  );
}

patterns.name: intelligence-panel
patterns.intent: An AI assistant panel — a scrollable message thread with an assistant avatar, a text composer with a send action, suggested-prompt chips, and streaming/loading states.
patterns.description: The sanctioned way to surface an AI assistant beside the app: a `Drawer` anchored to the right edge whose body is a `ScrollArea` message thread (each assistant turn led by an `Avatar`), a footer composer built from `InputTextArea` plus a send `ButtonIcon`, and a row of suggested-prompt `Chip`s that seed the composer. Streaming is expressed with a `Spinner` on the in-flight assistant turn; a `Separator` divides the thread from the composer. Composes existing components — the conversation UI is a recipe, not a bespoke chat widget.
when_to_use: An in-app AI assistant / copilot that stays available beside the current task.
A conversational thread that streams responses and offers starter prompts.
Keeping the assistant non-blocking — the user can dismiss it and keep working.
when_not_to_use: A one-shot prompt with a single answer — use an inline field, not a threaded panel.
A blocking, full-attention flow — use a `Dialog`.
Static help content with no conversation — a plain `Drawer` or docs link is enough.
anti_patterns: Hand-rolling a fixed side panel instead of composing `Drawer` (loses focus trap, scroll lock, ARIA, animations).
Auto-scrolling the thread on every token without pinning to bottom — the user loses their place while reading history.
Disabling the whole panel while streaming instead of showing a `Spinner` on the pending turn and keeping the composer usable.
Rendering suggested prompts as bare buttons rather than `Chip`s, breaking the kit's affordance for dismissible/selectable hints.

patterns.name: sheet-detail-panel
patterns.intent: Show the details of a selected item in a side Sheet — title, key/value properties, content states, and footer actions.
patterns.description: The sanctioned way to present "details of the selected thing" beside its list: a `Sheet` anchored to the right edge with a header (title + close), a body that renders either a key/value property list or a content state (loading → Spinner, empty/error → Empty), and a footer of actions. This is the React composition of the Vue kit's feature-rich `Details` component — its content-state, properties, and action-bar behavior become a composed recipe rather than props baked into the Sheet primitive.
when_to_use: Inspecting/acting on a selected row or entity next to its table or list.
A detail view that must load, can be empty, and offers a few actions.
when_not_to_use: A centered confirmation or short form — use `Dialog`.
Persistent, non-modal page chrome — use `SidebarSecondary`, not a modal Sheet.
A simple message with no data/actions — a plain `Sheet` is enough.
anti_patterns: Hand-rolling a fixed side panel instead of composing `Sheet` (loses focus trap, scroll lock, ARIA, animations).
Rendering a spinner/empty state inline in the body INSTEAD of switching the whole body by a `contentState` — mixed states confuse.
Putting more than ~2–3 primary actions in the footer; overflow belongs in a menu.
Omitting `SheetTitle` — the panel then has no accessible name.

function DetailPanel({ open, onOpenChange, contentState, item }) { return ( {item?.name ?? 'Details'} {contentState === 'loading' ? (
) : contentState === 'empty' ? ( Nothing to show This item has no details yet. ) : ( {item.properties.map((p) => ( {p.label} {p.value} ))} )} Close} /> ); }

patterns.name: sidebar-navigation
patterns.intent: The two-tier app navigation — a collapsed primary icon rail of top-level areas beside an expandable secondary section panel, with drill-down for nested items.
patterns.description: The sanctioned composition for the kit's primary navigation: a `SidebarPrimary` icon rail listing top-level product areas, and a `SidebarSecondary` panel showing the sections of the active area. `SidebarSecondary`'s built-in `SidebarSecondaryMenuSub` handles one level of drill-down; use `Collapsible` sections for grouped links and a `Tree` when the section is a deep, arbitrarily-nested hierarchy. Where the top-level areas read better as a horizontal bar than a rail, `NavigationMenu` is the sanctioned alternative for that tier. This is the nav composition itself — not the page frame around it.
when_to_use: An application with several top-level areas, each holding its own sections.
Navigation that must stay visible and persistent while the user works.
A section list deep enough to need drill-down (submenus) or a hierarchy (Tree).
when_not_to_use: The whole application frame (header + rails + main region) — that is the `app-shell` pattern; this composes only the nav that lives inside it.
A flat handful of destinations with no nesting — a single menu or `NavigationMenu` bar is enough; skip the two-tier rail.
Transient, task-scoped navigation — use tabs or an overlay, not persistent chrome.
anti_patterns: Rebuilding the icon rail or section panel by hand instead of composing `SidebarPrimary` / `SidebarSecondary` (loses collapse state, active-item wiring, ARIA).
Nesting a `Tree` inside every section when one drill-down level via `SidebarSecondaryMenuSub` would do — reserve `Tree` for genuinely deep hierarchies.
Duplicating the primary areas as both a rail AND a top `NavigationMenu` — pick one home for the top tier.
Putting page content or actions in the sidebars instead of the main region.

patterns.name: table-view
patterns.intent: A full list/table screen — a page header, a search + filter toolbar, and a paginated DataTable of records.
patterns.description: The sanctioned shape for a records screen: a `PageHeader` (title + primary action), a toolbar pairing an `InputSearch` for free-text with `Filter` triggers for discrete criteria, and a `DataTable` rendering the rows with its built-in `DataTablePagination`. This is the canonical "list of things" layout — compose it rather than assembling a bespoke table page. For row selection with a contextual action bar, see `data-table-bulk-actions`, which layers selection onto this same table.
when_to_use: A primary screen listing records the user browses, searches, filters, and paginates.
A table that needs both free-text search (InputSearch) and discrete filters (Filter).
Any place the app shows "all the Xs" as the main content of a route.
when_not_to_use: Rows that need multi-select plus a bulk-action bar — use `data-table-bulk-actions`.
A small, fixed set of rows with no search/filter/pagination — a plain `Table` is enough.
Card-based catalog/gallery tiles rather than tabular rows — use `card-grid`.
anti_patterns: Reimplementing sorting/pagination by hand instead of using `DataTable` + `DataTablePagination`.
Using `InputSearch` for discrete-value filtering (status, type) — those belong in `Filter`, not free-text.
Omitting the `PageHeader` so the screen has no title or home for its primary action.
Placing per-row selection checkboxes here without the bulk-action bar — if you need selection, adopt `data-table-bulk-actions`.

patterns.name: wizard-dialog
patterns.intent: A multi-step flow inside a modal Dialog — a step/progress indicator, per-step form content, and Back / Next / Finish navigation.
patterns.description: The sanctioned way to run a short, guided multi-step task without leaving the page: a `Dialog` whose header carries a `Progress` step indicator, whose body swaps `Form` content per step, and whose footer navigates with Back / Next and a final Finish. The dialog stays mounted across steps so entered values persist; only the visible step's fields change. Reserve it for flows that are genuinely staged — 2 to a few steps — where splitting the input reduces cognitive load.
when_to_use: A guided setup/onboarding with 2–a few discrete steps in a fixed order.
Breaking a longer form into digestible stages with a visible progress cue.
A flow where later steps depend on earlier answers but the whole thing is short.
when_not_to_use: A single step — use `form-dialog`.
A long or branching linear flow better as a full-page route with its own URL per step.
A yes/no confirmation — use `confirm-dialog`.
anti_patterns: Remounting the dialog (or unmounting steps) between steps so entered data is lost — keep it mounted and preserve state.
Hiding progress so the user can't tell how many steps remain — always show the `Progress` indicator.
Allowing Next while the current step is invalid — gate advancement on the step's `Form` validation.
Cramming every field into one step and faking a wizard — if it's one step, it's a `form-dialog`.
